questions.question: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in JavaScript, and how do you handle it in real code?
questions.answer: Because every number is an IEEE-754 double stored in binary. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so each is stored as a value slightly above or below the decimal it looks like. Adding them yields 0.30000000000000004, which of course is not exactly 0.3. You never fix this by rounding the type; you fix it by choosing the right technique: compare with a tolerance (Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON, or a scaled tolerance for larger magnitudes), format only for display with toFixed/toLocaleString, and for money store integer paise/cents (Math.round(rupees * 100)) so all arithmetic stays in exact integers. Never compare floats with === when they came out of arithmetic.
key_points: All numbers are 64-bit binary floats — decimals like 0.1 are not exact
0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so strict equality fails
Compare with Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON or a scaled tolerance
Money should be stored as integer paise/cents, not floats
toFixed/toLocaleString are for display, not for fixing the underlying value

questions.answer:
Output: 10, NaN, 16, 1900, 5.

parseInt and parseFloat read from the left and stop at the first character that cannot continue a number, so "10px" yields 10 and the junk is ignored. Number is strict: the entire string must be numeric after trimming, so "10px" is NaN. parseInt without a radix auto-detects: the "0x" prefix means hex, so "0x10" is 16 — this is why you should always pass 10 as the radix. parseFloat does understand exponent notation, so "1.9e3" is 1900, whereas parseInt stops at the dot and returns 1. Finally parseInt stringifies its argument first: String(0.0000005) is "5e-7", so parseInt reads 5.
key_points: parseInt/parseFloat stop at the first invalid character; Number is strict
parseInt without a radix auto-detects 0x as hexadecimal
parseFloat understands exponents (1.9e3 → 1900); parseInt does not
parseInt stringifies first, so parseInt(0.0000005) is 5
Always pass radix 10: parseInt(value, 10)

questions.question: What is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and why do large database IDs get sent to the frontend as strings?
questions.answer: MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991, or 2^53 - 1. Above that, doubles can no longer represent every integer, so two different integers can map to the same stored value. The failure happens at parse time: the literal 9007199254740993 becomes 9007199254740992 before any code runs, and Number.isSafeInteger returns false. REST APIs therefore serialize 64-bit IDs (Twitter snowflake IDs, some Postgres bigints) as JSON strings, because JSON numbers would be silently corrupted in the browser. The frontend keeps them as strings and never does arithmetic on them, or converts to BigInt when it truly must compute.
key_points: Above it adjacent integers collapse to the same double
The corruption happens when the literal/JSON number is parsed
APIs send 64-bit IDs as strings; use BigInt for real arithmetic
Month is 0-indexed; day 0 means the last day of the previous month
Date normalises overflow instead of throwing
setMonth on the 31st rolls into the next month
Clamp with Math.min(day, lastDayOfTargetMonth)
2026 is not a leap year: 29 Feb becomes 1 Mar

questions.question: What are the rules and limits of BigInt? Why does JSON.stringify({ id: 1n }) throw?
questions.answer: BigInt represents arbitrary-precision integers, written 10n or BigInt(10). typeof is 'bigint'. Arithmetic works, but division truncates toward zero (10n / 3n is 3n), and mixing with a Number throws TypeError ('Cannot mix BigInt and other types') — you must convert explicitly with BigInt(n) or Number(big). Math methods do not accept BigInt, and there is no implicit conversion in either direction because both would silently lose information. JSON has no BigInt type, so JSON.stringify throws TypeError on a BigInt; the standard workaround is to serialize it as a string (id: id.toString()) and parse it back with BigInt(str). Comparisons like 10n > 5 are allowed, since ordering does not lose precision.
key_points: Written 10n; typeof is 'bigint'
Integer division truncates: 10n / 3n === 3n
Mixing BigInt and Number throws — convert explicitly
No Math methods on BigInt
JSON.stringify throws; serialize as a string
